e.t: “Swallowed” describes the action of taking something in so that it is engulfed or overwhelmed. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word is used for things being swallowed up, sometimes as a physical image and sometimes for destruction expressed in the same way. It occurs 50 times in 48 verses. The central picture is complete absorption or being overwhelmed, while the surrounding verse determines what is swallowed and how literally the image is used.

“Medicine” refers to something used as a treatment for sickness or bodily distress. In this Hebrew Old Testament word, it functions as a noun: it names the treatment itself rather than an action or person. The word occurs once in the Hebrew corpus, at Proverbs 17:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is medicine.

Edrei is a place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, consistently rendered "Edrei." The name occurs in accounts and lists connected with Israel’s movements and territory, including Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is primarily the location it identifies; the surrounding verse supplies the specific event or geographic detail associated with it.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Proverbs 19:19. The available wording does not provide a clear English gloss or short definition, so its precise lexical meaning cannot be stated more specifically here without going beyond the biblical evidence. Its role must therefore be understood from the full sentence and surrounding passage rather than from this word in isolation.

Because it is a name, its meaning in a particular passage depends chiefly on which person named Gershom is being identified.

This word refers to Dinhabah, a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It is rendered “Dinhabah” and appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 36:32 and 1 Chronicles 1:43. Those passages preserve the same name, while the available lexical information does not provide a separate definition or explain the name’s underlying meaning. Its role is therefore best understood as identifying Dinhabah within the genealogical and historical record, rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “hooks,” naming a physical fitting used in the tabernacle’s construction. It appears 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, where it is associated with the curtains, pillars, sockets, and courtyard structures. The word functions as a concrete noun for these connecting or hanging pieces rather than describing an action or quality. Its repeated use in the construction instructions shows a practical object needed to assemble and secure the sanctuary’s parts.

This Hebrew word functions as a predicate, expressing that something “is.” It helps connect a subject with a statement about it, rather than naming an object or describing an action by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what subject and statement it joins, but its basic role is to affirm or identify what something is.

This Hebrew word means “destroyed.” It functions as a verb, describing an action that brings something to an end. In its six Old Testament occurrences, the word refers to the condition or result of something being destroyed, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is affected and who or what carries out the action. Its use appears in Ezra and Daniel, so its basic sense remains consistent across those passages even though each verse supplies its own context.

This Hebrew word refers to a “circle,” describing a rounded form or circular extent. It appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its uses include descriptions associated with the created world and the surrounding expanse, while the central idea remains a circular shape or area. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “mightily,” expressing that an action is carried out with great strength or force. It functions as an adverbial description, showing how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages describing forceful action, strong speech, repair work, and earnest behavior. Its precise emphasis depends on the action it modifies in each sentence.

This Hebrew verb means “divided.” It describes separating something into portions or distributing it among people or groups. In the Old Testament, it is used for dividing land, arranging people or families into assigned portions, and sharing something fairly among those involved. The word occurs 65 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it can describe both physical separation and the orderly apportioning of responsibilities or possessions. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being divided and who receives each portion.

This Hebrew word refers to “archers,” people who shoot with bows. It functions as a noun naming such people rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, appearing in Judges, Job, and Proverbs. Its central sense is therefore a group or class of bowmen. The surrounding verse determines how that reference functions in each passage, but the word itself points to archers as people identified by their use of bows.

This Hebrew word means “singed,” describing something affected by heat without stating more about the surrounding event. It functions as a descriptive word for a condition or result. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 3:27. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its basic sense remains “singed.”

Telaim is a proper name, functioning as the name of a specific place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 15:4, and is rendered “Telaim.” The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the place or its role in that passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “earth” and functions as a noun naming the earth. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 2:10. The surrounding verse determines its precise role in that passage.

e.t: Joah is a personal name, identifying a specific man rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is consistently rendered “Joah” and appears eleven times across ten verses. The name is associated with several individuals in the historical records, including people connected with royal service, worship, and family lines. Its precise identity depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal function is simply to name a person.

This Hebrew verb expresses an action, but its specific meaning cannot be determined from the available lexical information alone. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Proverbs 20:25, and no explicit definition or approved meaning term is available. The word functions as the predicate connected with a person and matters involving a sacred vow or offering, but the precise action should not be reconstructed without the verse text and surrounding context.

This Hebrew noun refers to “beasts,” naming creatures rather than people. It appears three times in the Old Testament, each time in prophetic passages. The word identifies beings described as beasts within those passages, while the surrounding verse determines the precise setting and force of the reference. This Hebrew word means “able,” describing someone who can do what is being considered. It functions as a descriptive word, presenting a person as able in a particular matter rather than naming the action itself. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, and its English rendering is consistently “able.” Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is being able to do something.

This Hebrew word describes something as “perfect.” It serves as a describing word, presenting the person or thing in view as having the quality of perfection. Within the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs two times, both in Ezekiel 27. Its use is therefore limited in the available text, but the repeated sense remains clear: it identifies what is being described as perfect. This Hebrew word means “almond,” naming a specific natural object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 30:37, so its use is limited to that single passage. The word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and scene. It functions as a concrete noun rather than expressing an action, quality, or command. Thus, when encountered in the Bible, it identifies an almond without requiring a broader theological meaning to be added.

Its precise force in Isaiah depends on the sentence and context in which the number is mentioned.

This Hebrew word means "shut." It functions as an action word, expressing the condition or action of something being shut. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Daniel 6:22. This Hebrew verb means “harden.” It describes the action of making something hard or firm. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 6:10. Because it is a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. This Hebrew word refers to a “census,” an organized count of people. It names the census itself rather than describing a person or action. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning points to an official accounting or listing of people.

Abel is a Hebrew place-name, referring to a location rather than describing an action or quality. It appears four times in the Old Testament corpus, with three occurrences in 2 Samuel and one in 1 Samuel. The English rendering consistently gives “Abel,” supporting its use as a proper name. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the location’s role there.

Achar is a Hebrew personal name, rendered in English as “Achar.” It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament data, at 1 Chronicles 2:7. No short definition or verse text is available here; therefore, the specific significance attached to Achar in that passage cannot be explained from the word alone.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name "Cain," identifying a particular man rather than describing a general quality or action. Its scriptural use consistently functions as a person’s name within genealogical and narrative references. The surrounding passages are needed to explain what Cain does or what happens to him in any particular verse.

This Hebrew word refers to “horns,” functioning as a concrete naming term rather than an abstract idea or action. It occurs four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, with three occurrences in Exodus 34 and one in Psalm 69. Its repeated use in Exodus connects it with the description of Moses’ face, while Psalm 69 provides another occurrence of the same word. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force in each passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “Melech,” functioning as a name or designation rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both occurrences appearing in Zechariah 7:2. Because the available wording does not provide a fuller definition or surrounding verse text, the safest understanding is simply that it identifies Melech in that passage. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “behave.” It functions as a predicate, describing what someone does rather than naming a person or object. It occurs four times in the Old Testament, in passages involving people and their dealings with others. Its use in Proverbs 6:3 and Isaiah 3:5 shows that it can describe conduct within human relationships and social situations, while its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This word is a proper place-name: “Ramathaimzophim.” It identifies a named place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, with both occurrences appearing in 1 Samuel 1:1. Because the available wording preserves the name rather than giving an explanatory definition, the surrounding verse is needed to understand what is being said about that place within the sentence.

Shobai is a Hebrew personal name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a person in the Old Testament and is preserved as “Shobai” in the English renderings. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Bible corpus, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Because no explicit definition or broader lexical sense is provided, the safest understanding is simply that Shobai is the individual’s name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. e.t: “Shuthelah” is a personal name, referring to a person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, all in genealogical records in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. The name is associated with family descent and with a birth or begetting relationship in the genealogy. Scripture preserves it as a proper name, so its ordinary meaning is the individual identified by that name, not a general concept or translated description.

This Hebrew word means “wise,” describing a person, conduct, or judgment marked by wisdom. It can function in a sentence to characterize someone as wise or to describe wise action. In the Old Testament, it occurs 63 times, appearing in passages connected with instruction, leadership, understanding, and prudent conduct. Its use therefore reaches beyond possessing knowledge: it commonly identifies wisdom expressed in how someone acts or responds. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “heaven” and refers to the realm or expanse above the earth. It is used throughout the Old Testament for what God made, what lies above, and what is associated with God’s rule and activity. The word occurs 421 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it is a broad and regularly used description rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “drink.” It describes the action of taking liquid, whether people or animals are involved, and may be used when someone is being provided with liquid. The word occurs 62 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring everyday action across the biblical text. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Tanhumeth is a personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a general description or action. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 2 Kings 25:23 and once in Jeremiah 40:8. Because the available rendering preserves the name rather than translating it into an ordinary English meaning, its significance here is its role in identifying a person. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s specific actions or circumstances.
